etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: Inherited from Middle English rhetorik, rhetoric, borrowed from Old French rhetorique, borrowed from Latin rhētorica, borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥητορικὴ (rhētorikḕ), ellipsis of ῥητορῐκή τέχνη (rhētorĭkḗ tékhnē).
senses: The art of using language, especially public speaking, as a means to persuade.
(sometimes derogatory) Meaningless language with an exaggerated style intended to impress.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
paragraphs: Inherited from Middle English rhetorik, borrowed from Old French rhetorique, borrowed from Latin rhētoricus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós), from ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, “public speaker”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós). By surface analysis, rhetor +‎ -ic.
